*Translator's note:* *Heb* “These are the words.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “on the other side of the Jordan.” This would appear to favor authorship by someone living on the west side of the Jordan, that is, in Canaan, whereas the biblical tradition locates Moses on the east side (cf. v. {{Deuteronomy 1:5|5}}). However the Hebrew phrase בְּעֵבֶר הַיַּרְדֵּן (beʿever hayyarden) is a frozen form meaning “Transjordan,” a name appropriate from any geographical vantage point. To this day, one standing east of the Jordan can describe himself as being in Transjordan.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew term מוֹל (mol) may also mean “in front of” or “near” (cf. NCV, TEV, CEV, NLT).

*Study note:* This place is otherwise unattested and its location is unknown. Perhaps it is Khirbet Sufah, 4 mi (6 km) SSE of Madaba, Jordan.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew term בֵּין (ben) may suggest “in the area of.”

*Study note:* *Paran* is the well-known desert area between Mount Sinai and Kadesh Barnea (cf. {{Numbers 10:12|Num 10:12}}; {{Numbers 12:16|12:16}}).

*Study note:* *Tophel* refers possibly to eṭ-Ṭafîleh, 15 mi (25 km) SE of the Dead Sea, or to Dâbîlu, another name for Paran. See H. Cazelles, “Tophel ({{Deuteronomy 1:1|Deut. 1:1}}),” *VT* 9 (1959): 412-15.

*Study note:* *Laban*. Perhaps this refers to Libnah ({{Numbers 33:20|Num 33:20}}).

*Study note:* *Hazeroth*. This probably refers to ʿAin Khadra. See Y. Aharoni, *The Land of the Bible*, 199-200.

*Study note:* *Di Zahab*. Perhaps this refers to Mina al-Dhahab on the eastern Sinai coast.

*Study note:* *An eleven-day journey* was about 140 mi (233 km).

*Study note:* *Horeb* is another name for Sinai. “Horeb” occurs 9 times in the Book of Deuteronomy and “Sinai” only once ({{Deuteronomy 33:2|33:2}}). “Sinai” occurs 13 times in the Book of Exodus and “Horeb” only 3 times.

*Study note:* *Kadesh Barnea*. Possibly this refers to ʿAin Qudeis, about 50 mi (80 km) southwest of Beer Sheba, but more likely to ʿAin Qudeirat, 5 mi (8 km) NW of ʿAin Qudeis. See R. Cohen, “Did I Excavate Kadesh Barnea?” *BAR* 7 (1981): 20-33.

*Study note:* *Mount Seir* is synonymous with Edom. “By way of Mount Seir” refers to the route from Horeb that ended up in Edom Cf. CEV “by way of the Mount Seir Road”; TEV “by way of the hill country of Edom.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in” or “on.” Here there is a contrast between the ordinary time of eleven days (v. {{Deuteronomy 1:2|2}}) and the actual time of forty years, so “not until” brings out that vast disparity.

*Study note:* The *eleventh month* is Shebat in the Hebrew calendar, January/February in the modern (Gregorian) calendar.

*Study note:* The *fortieth year* would be 1406 b.c. according to the “early” date of the exodus. See E. H. Merrill, *Kingdom of Priests*, 66-75.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “according to all which.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “when he struck [or “smote”].”

*Study note:* See {{Deuteronomy 2:26|Deut 2:26-3:22}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “who lived.”

*Study note:* *Heshbon* is probably modern Tell Hesban, about 7.5 mi (12 km) south southwest of Amman, Jordan.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “who lived.”

*Study note:* *Ashtaroth* is probably Tell ʿAshtarah, about 22 mi (35 km) due east of the Sea of Galilee.

*Study note:* *Edrei* is probably modern Derʿa, 60 mi (95 km) south of Damascus (see {{Numbers 21:33|Num 21:33}}; {{Joshua 12:4|Josh 12:4}}; {{Joshua 13:12|13:12}}, {{Joshua 13:31|31}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “this instruction”; KJV, NIV, NRSV “this law”; TEV “God’s laws and teachings.” The Hebrew noun תּוֹרָה (torah) is derived from the verb יָרָה (yarah, “to teach”) and here it refers to the Book of Deuteronomy, not the Pentateuch as a whole.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “turn”; NAB “Leave here”; NIV, TEV “Break camp.”

*Study note:* As a geographic feature the rift valley (עֲרָבָה, ʿaravah) extends from Galilee to the Gulf of Aqaba. The reference here probably includes the Jordan Valley and continues to the wider part of the rift valley below the Dead Sea. Some versions transliterate the name as Arabah (ASV, NAB, NIV, NRSV).

*Translator's note:* The שְׁפֵלָה (shephelah) is the geographical region between the Mediterranean coastal plain and the hill country, sometimes called the “western foothills” (NIV, CEV, NLT), “Judean foothills” (HCSB), “lowland” (NASB, ESV), or by the Hebrew “Shephelah” (NRSV).

*Study note:* The Negev is the area of central, southern Judah, south of the hill country and Beer Sheba and west of the rift valley. As a geographic feature it is a depression extending south to the gulf of Aqaba, but the reference here is probably to the northern portion of the region.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I have placed before you the land.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the Lord.” Since the Lord is speaking, it is preferable for clarity to supply the first person pronoun in the translation.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “swore” (so NAB, NIV, NRSV, NLT). This refers to God’s promise, made by solemn oath, to give the patriarchs the land.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “fathers” (also in vv. {{Deuteronomy 1:11|11}}, {{Deuteronomy 1:21|21}}, {{Deuteronomy 1:35|35}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “their seed after them.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “multiplied you.”

*Translator's note:* Or “heavens.” The Hebrew term שָׁמַיִם (shamayim) may be translated “heaven(s)” or “sky” depending on the context.
*Translator's note:* The Hebrew verb נְבֹנִים (nevonim, from בִּין [bin]) is a Niphal referring to skill or intelligence (see T. Fretheim, *NIDOTTE* 1:652-53).

*Translator's note:* Or “you.” A number of English versions treat the remainder of this verse and v. {{Deuteronomy 1:17|17}} as direct discourse rather than indirect discourse (cf. KJV, NAB, NIV, NRSV, NLT).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “brothers.” The term “brothers” could, in English, be understood to refer to siblings, so “fellow citizens” has been used in the translation.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew word צֶדֶק (tsedeq, “fairly”) carries the basic idea of conformity to a norm of expected behavior or character, one established by God himself. Fair judgment adheres strictly to that norm or standard (see D. Reimer, *NIDOTTE* 3:750).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “between a man and his brother.” The first use of “brother” in this verse refers broadly to fellow citizens. This second use is narrower, being in opposition to the “resident foreigner.” The גֵּר (ger) “resident foreigner” was not simply a foreigner (Hebrew נֵכָר; nekar) but was essentially a naturalized citizen and had equal protection under the law. This is one of the verses designed to ensure that equal treatment (see also {{Deuteronomy 10:16|Deut 10:16-19}}; {{Deuteronomy 16:18|16:18-20}}; {{Exodus 12:49|Exod 12:49}}; {{Numbers 15:16|Num 15:16}}, {{Numbers 15:29|29}}).

*Study note:* On the Hebrew ger (גֵּר) “resident foreigner,” see notes at {{Exodus 12:19|Exod 12:19}} and {{Deuteronomy 29:11|Deut 29:11}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “you,” and throughout the verse (cf. NASB, NRSV).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the small,” but referring to social status, not physical stature.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew participle has an imminent future sense here, although many English versions treat it as a present tense (“is giving us,” NAB, NIV, NRSV) or a predictive future (“will give us,” NCV).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the Lord your God.” The pronoun (“he”) has been used in the translation for stylistic reasons, to avoid repetition.

*Translator's note:* Or “has given you the land” (cf. NAB, NIV, NRSV).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the thing was good in my eyes.”

*Translator's note:* Or “selected” (so NIV, NRSV, TEV); *Heb* “took.”

*Translator's note:* Or “the Wadi Eshcol” (so NAB).

*Study note:* The *Eshcol Valley* is a verdant valley near Hebron, still famous for its viticulture (cf. {{Numbers 13:22|Num 13:22-23}}). The Hebrew name “Eshcol” means “trestle,” that is, the frame on which grape vines grow.
*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text includes “in their hand,” which is unnecessary and somewhat redundant in English style.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the mouth of the Lord your God.” To include “the mouth” would make for odd English style. The mouth stands by metonymy for the Lord’s command, which in turn represents the Lord himself.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in your tents,” that is, privately.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “have caused our hearts to melt.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “greater.” Many English versions understand this to refer to physical size or strength rather than numbers (cf. “stronger,” NAB, NIV, NRSV; “bigger,” NASB).

*Translator's note:* Or “as the sky.” The Hebrew term שָׁמַיִם (shamayim) may be translated “heaven(s)” or “sky” depending on the context.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “we have seen.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the sons of the Anakim.”

*Study note:* *Anakites* were giant people ({{Numbers 13:33|Num 13:33}}; {{Deuteronomy 2:10|Deut 2:10}}, {{Deuteronomy 2:21|21}}; {{Deuteronomy 9:2|9:2}}) descended from a certain Anak whose own forefather Arba founded the city of Kiriath Arba, i.e., Hebron ({{Joshua 21:11|Josh 21:11}}).
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “do not tremble and do not be afraid.” Two synonymous commands are combined for emphasis.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew participle indicates imminent future action here, though some English versions treat it as a predictive future (“will go ahead of you,” NCV; cf. also TEV, CEV).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “according to all which he did for you in Egypt before your eyes.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the Lord your God.” The pronoun (“him”) has been employed in the translation for stylistic reasons.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and swore,” i.e., made an oath or vow.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Not a man among these men.”

*Study note:* *Caleb* had, with Joshua, brought back to Israel a minority report from Canaan urging a conquest of the land, for he was confident of the Lord’s power ({{Numbers 13:6|Num 13:6}}, {{Numbers 13:8|8}}, {{Numbers 13:16|16}}, {{Numbers 13:30|30}}; {{Numbers 14:30|14:30}}, {{Numbers 14:38|38}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the Lord.” The pronoun (“me”) has been employed in the translation, since it sounds strange to an English reader for the Lord to speak about himself in third person.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the one who stands before you”; NAB “your aide”; TEV “your helper.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “it”; the referent (the land) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “would be a prey.”

*Study note:* *Do not know good from bad*. This is a figure of speech called a merism (suggesting a whole by referring to its extreme opposites). Other examples are the tree of “the knowledge of good and evil” ({{Genesis 2:9|Gen 2:9}}), the boy who knows enough “to reject the wrong and choose the right” ({{Isaiah 7:16|Isa 7:16}}; {{Isaiah 8:4|8:4}}), and those who “cannot tell their right hand from their left” ({{Jonah 4:11|Jonah 4:11}}). A young child is characterized by lack of knowledge.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew pronoun is plural, as are the following verbs, indicating that Moses and the people are addressed (note v. {{Deuteronomy 1:41|41}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the Reed Sea.” “Reed” is a better translation of the Hebrew סוּף (suf), traditionally rendered “red.” The name “Red Sea” is based on the LXX which referred to it as ἐρυθρᾶς θαλάσσης (eruthras thalassēs, “red sea”). Nevertheless, because the body of water in question is known in modern times as the Red Sea, this term was used in the translation. The part of the Red Sea in view here is not the one crossed in the exodus but its eastern arm, now known as the Gulf of Eilat or Gulf of Aqaba.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the mouth of the Lord.” See note at {{Deuteronomy 1:26|1:26}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in that hill country,” repeating the end of v. {{Deuteronomy 1:43|43}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “came out to meet.”

*Study note:* *Hormah* is probably Khirbet el-Meshash, 5.5 mi (9 km) west of Arad and 7.5 mi (12 km) SE of Beer Sheba. Its name is a derivative of the verb חָרָם (kharam, “to ban; to exterminate”). See {{Numbers 21:3|Num 21:3}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the Lord.” The pronoun (“he”) has been employed in the translation here for stylistic reasons, to avoid redundancy.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “did not hear your voice and did not turn an ear to you.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “like the days which you lived.” This refers to the rest of the forty-year period in the desert before Israel arrived in Moab.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Reed Sea.” See note on the term “Red Sea” in {{Deuteronomy 1:40|Deut 1:40}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “command” (so KJV, NASB); NRSV “charge the people as follows.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “brothers”; NAB “your kinsmen.”

*Study note:* *The descendants of Esau* (*Heb* “sons of Esau”; the phrase also occurs in {{Deuteronomy 2:8|2:8}}, {{Deuteronomy 2:12|12}}, {{Deuteronomy 2:22|22}}, {{Deuteronomy 2:29|29}}). These are the inhabitants of the land otherwise known as Edom, south and east of the Dead Sea. Jacob’s brother Esau had settled there after his bitter strife with Jacob ({{Genesis 36:1|Gen 36:1-8}}). “Edom” means “reddish,” probably because of the red sandstone of the region, but also by popular etymology because Esau, at birth, was reddish ({{Genesis 25:25|Gen 25:25}}).
*Study note:* *Mount Seir* is synonymous with Edom.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text does not have the first person pronoun; it has been supplied for purposes of English style (the Lord is speaking here).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “all the work of your hands.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he has.” This has been converted to first person in the translation in keeping with English style.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “known” (so ASV, NASB); NAB “been concerned about.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the Lord your God has.” This has been replaced in the translation by the first person pronoun (“I”) in keeping with English style.

*Translator's note:* Or “brothers”; NRSV “our kin.”

*Study note:* As a geographic feature the rift valley (עֲרָבָה, ʿaravah) extends from the Gulf of Aqaba to Galilee. Traveling up the middle of the rift valley probably would have been the easiest path, at least up to the Dead Sea.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from.”

*Study note:* *Elat* was a port city at the head of the eastern arm of the Red Sea, that is, the Gulf of Aqaba (or Gulf of Eilat). Solomon ({{1 Kings 9:28|1 Kgs 9:28}}), Uzziah ({{2 Kings 14:22|2 Kgs 14:22}}), and Ahaz ({{2 Kings 16:5|2 Kgs 16:5-6}}) used it as a port but eventually it became permanently part of Edom. It may be what is known today as Tell el-Kheleifeh. Modern Eilat is located farther west along the northern coast. See G. Pratico, “Nelson Glueck’s 1938-1940 Excavations at Tell el-Kheleifeh: A Reappraisal,” *BASOR* 259 (1985): 1-32.

*Study note:* *Ezion Geber*. A place near the Gulf of Aqaba, Ezion-geber must be distinguished from Elat (cf. {{1 Kings 9:26|1 Kgs 9:26-28}}; 2 Chr 8:17-18). It was, however, also a port city ({{1 Kings 22:48|1 Kgs 22:48-49}}). It may be the same as the modern site Gezirat al-Fauran, 15 mi (24 km) south-southwest from Tell el-Kheleifah.

*Study note:* *Ar* was a Moabite city on the Arnon River east of the Dead Sea. It is mentioned elsewhere in the “Book of the Wars of Yahweh” ({{Numbers 21:15|Num 21:15}}; cf. {{Numbers 21:28|21:28}}; {{Isaiah 15:1|Isa 15:1}}). Here it is synonymous with the whole land of Moab.

*Study note:* *The descendants of Lot*. Following the destruction of the cities of the plain, Sodom and Gomorrah, as God’s judgment, Lot fathered two sons by his two daughters, namely, Moab and Ammon ({{Genesis 19:30|Gen 19:30-38}}). Thus, these descendants of Lot in and around Ar were the Moabites.

*Study note:* *Emites*. These giant people, like the Anakites ({{Deuteronomy 1:28|Deut 1:28}}), were also known as Rephaites (v. {{Deuteronomy 2:11|11}}). They appear elsewhere in the narrative of the invasion of the kings of the east where they are said to have lived around Shaveh Kiriathaim, perhaps 9 to 11 mi (15 to 18 km) east of the north end of the Dead Sea ({{Genesis 14:5|Gen 14:5}}).

*Study note:* *Rephaites*. The earliest reference to this infamous giant race is, again, in the story of the invasion of the eastern kings ({{Genesis 14:5|Gen 14:5}}). They lived around Ashteroth Karnaim, probably modern Tel Ashtarah (cf. {{Deuteronomy 1:4|Deut 1:4}}), in the Bashan plateau east of the Sea of Galilee. Og, king of Bashan, was a Rephaite ({{Deuteronomy 3:11|Deut 3:11}}; {{Joshua 12:4|Josh 12:4}}; {{Joshua 13:12|13:12}}). Other texts speak of them or their kinfolk in both Transjordan ({{Deuteronomy 2:20|Deut 2:20}}; {{Deuteronomy 3:13|3:13}}) and Canaan ({{Joshua 11:21|Josh 11:21-22}}; {{Joshua 14:12|14:12}}, {{Joshua 14:15|15}}; {{Joshua 15:13|15:13-14}}; {{Judges 1:20|Judg 1:20}}; {{1 Samuel 17:4|1 Sam 17:4}}; 1 Chr 20:4-8). They also appear in extra-biblical literature, especially in connection with the city state of Ugarit. See C. L’Heureux, “Ugaritic and Biblical Rephaim,” *HTR* 67 (1974): 265-74.

*Study note:* *Horites*. Most likely these are the same as the well-known people of ancient Near Eastern texts described as Hurrians. They were geographically widespread and probably non-Semitic. Genesis speaks of them as the indigenous peoples of Edom that Esau expelled ({{Genesis 36:8|Gen 36:8-19}}, {{Genesis 36:31|31-43}}) and also as among those who confronted the kings of the east ({{Genesis 14:6|Gen 14:6}}).

*Translator's note:* Most modern English versions, beginning with the ASV (1901), regard vv. {{Deuteronomy 2:10|10-12}} as parenthetical to the narrative.

*Study note:* *Wadi Zered*. Now known as Wadi el-Ḥesa, this valley marked the boundary between Moab to the north and Edom to the south.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “we crossed the Wadi Zered.” This has been translated as “we did so” for stylistic reasons, to avoid redundancy.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from the middle of.” Although many recent English versions leave this expression untranslated, the point seems to be that these soldiers did not die in battle but “within the camp.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and it was when they were eliminated, all the men of war, to die from the midst of the people.”
*Study note:* *Ar*. See note on this word in {{Deuteronomy 2:9|Deut 2:9}}.
*Study note:* *Lot’s descendants*. See note on this phrase in {{Deuteronomy 2:9|Deut 2:9}}.

*Study note:* *Rephaites*. See note on this word in {{Deuteronomy 2:11|Deut 2:11}}.

*Study note:* *Zamzummites*. Just as the Moabites called Rephaites by the name Emites, the Ammonites called them Zamzummites (or Zazites; {{Genesis 14:5|Gen 14:5}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “them”; the referent (the Rephaites) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “them”; the referent (the Ammonites) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Study note:* *Avvites*. Otherwise unknown, these people were probably also Anakite (or Rephaite) giants who lived in the lower Mediterranean coastal plain until they were expelled by the Caphtorites.

*Study note:* *Caphtorites*. These peoples are familiar from both the OT ({{Genesis 10:14|Gen 10:14}}; 1 Chr 1:12; Jer 47:4; {{Amos 9:7|Amos 9:7}}) and ancient Near Eastern texts (Miriam Lichtheim, *Ancient Egyptian Literature*, 2:37-38; *ANET* 138). They originated in Crete (OT “Caphtor”) and are identified as the ancestors of the Philistines ({{Genesis 10:14|Gen 10:14}}; Jer 47:4).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Caphtor”; the modern name of the island of Crete is used in the translation for clarity (cf. NCV, TEV, NLT).

*Study note:* *Heshbon* is the name of a prominent site (now Tel Hesbān, about 7.5 mi [12 km] south southwest of Amman, Jordan). Sihon made it his capital after having driven Moab from the area and forced them south to the Arnon ({{Numbers 21:26|Num 21:26-30}}). Heshbon is also mentioned in {{Deuteronomy 1:4|Deut 1:4}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “under heaven” (so NIV, NRSV).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “from before you.”
*Study note:* *Kedemoth*. This is probably Aleiyan, about 8 mi (13 km) north of the Arnon and between Dibon and Mattanah.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in the way in the way” (בַּדֶּרֶךְ בַּדֶּרֶךְ, badderekh badderekh). The repetition lays great stress on the idea of resolute determination to stick to the path. *IBHS* 116 §7.2.3c.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “silver.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and water for silver give to us so that I may drink.”

*Text-critical note:* The translation follows the LXX in reading the first person pronoun. The MT, followed by many English versions, has a second person masculine singular pronoun, “your.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “hardened his spirit” (so KJV, NASB, NRSV); NIV “made his spirit stubborn.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “made his heart obstinate” (so KJV, NASB); NRSV “made his heart defiant.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “into your hand.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “people.”

*Study note:* *Jahaz*. This is probably Khirbet el-Medeiyineh. See J. Dearman, “The Levitical Cities of Reuben and Moabite Toponymy,” *BASOR* 276 (1984): 55-57.

*Text-critical note:* The translation follows the *Qere* or marginal reading; the *Kethib* (consonantal text) has the singular, “his son.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “all his people.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “every city of men.” This apparently identifies the cities as inhabited.

*Study note:* *Divine judgment* refers to God’s designation of certain persons, places, and things as objects of his special wrath and judgment because, in his omniscience, he knows them to be impure and hopelessly unrepentant.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “under the ban” (נַחֲרֵם, nakharem). The verb employed is חָרַם (kharam, usually in the Hiphil) and the associated noun is חֵרֶם (kherem). See J. Naudé, *NIDOTTE*, 2:276-77, and, for a more thorough discussion, Susan Niditch, *War in the Hebrew Bible*, 28-77.

*Study note:* *Aroer*. Now known as ʿAraʾir on the northern edge of the Arnon river, Aroer marked the southern limit of Moab and, later, of the allotment of the tribe of Reuben ({{Joshua 13:9|Josh 13:9}}, {{Joshua 13:16|16}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the city in the wadi.” This enigmatic reference may refer to Ar or, more likely, to Aroer itself. Epexegetically the text might read, “From Aroer…, that is, the city in the wadi.” See D. L. Christensen, *{{Deuteronomy 1|Deuteronomy 1-11}}* (WBC), 49.
*Study note:* *Wadi Jabbok*. Now known as the Zerqa River, this is a major tributary of the Jordan that normally served as a boundary between Ammon and Gad ({{Deuteronomy 3:16|Deut 3:16}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “turned and went up.”

*Study note:* *Bashan*. This plateau country, famous for its oaks ({{Isaiah 2:13|Isa 2:13}}) and cattle ({{Deuteronomy 32:14|Deut 32:14}}; {{Amos 4:1|Amos 4:1}}), was north of Gilead along the Yarmuk River.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “people.”

*Study note:* *Edrei* is probably modern Derʿa, 60 mi (95 km) south of Damascus (see {{Numbers 21:33|Num 21:33}}; {{Joshua 12:4|Josh 12:4}}; {{Joshua 13:12|13:12}}, {{Joshua 13:31|31}}; also mentioned in {{Deuteronomy 1:4|Deut 1:4}}).
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “was left to him.” The final phrase “to him” is redundant in English and has been left untranslated.
*Study note:* *Argob*. This is a subdistrict of Bashan, perhaps north of the Yarmuk River. See Y. Aharoni, *Land of the Bible*, 314.

*Translator's note:* Or “high walls and barred gates” (NLT); *Heb* “high walls, gates, and bars.” Since “bars” could be understood to mean “saloons,” the qualifying adjective “locking” has been supplied in the translation.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew term פְּרָזִי (perazi) refers to rural areas, at the most “unwalled villages” (KJV, NASB “unwalled towns”).

*Study note:* *The divine curse*. See note on this phrase in {{Deuteronomy 2:34|Deut 2:34}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “we put them under the ban” (נַחֲרֵם, nakharem). See note at {{Deuteronomy 2:34|2:34}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “city of men.”
*Study note:* *Mount Hermon*. This is the famous peak at the southern end of the Anti-Lebanon mountain range known today as Jebel es-Sheik.

*Study note:* *Sidonians* were Phoenician inhabitants of the city of Sidon (now in Lebanon), about 47 mi (75 km) north of Mount Carmel.

*Study note:* *Sirion*. This name is attested in the Ugaritic texts as sryn. See *UT* 495.

*Study note:* *I invoke heaven and earth as witnesses against you*. This stock formula introduces what is known form-critically as a רִיב (riv) or controversy pattern. Since court proceedings required the testimony of witnesses, the Lord here summons heaven and earth (that is, all creation) to testify to his faithfulness, Israel’s disobedience, and the threat of judgment.

Just as “to love” (אָהֵב, ʾahev) means in a covenant context “to choose, obey,” so “to hate” (שָׂנֵא, saneʾ) means “to reject, disobey” (cf. the note on the word “loved” in {{Deuteronomy 4:37|Deut 4:37}}; see also {{Deuteronomy 5:10|5:10}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “visiting the sin of fathers upon sons and upon a third (generation) and upon a fourth (generation) of those who hate me.” God sometimes punishes children for the sins of a father (cf. {{Numbers 16:27|Num 16:27}}, {{Numbers 16:32|32}}; {{Joshua 7:24|Josh 7:24-25}}; {{2 Samuel 21:1|2 Sam 21:1-9}}). On the principle of corporate solidarity and responsibility in OT thought see J. Kaminsky, *Corporate Responsibility in the Hebrew Bible* (JSOTSup). In the idiom of the text, the father is the first generation and the “sons” the second generation, making grandsons the third and great-grandsons the fourth. The reference to a third and fourth generation is a way of emphasizing that the sinner’s punishment would last throughout his lifetime. In this culture, where men married and fathered children at a relatively young age, it would not be unusual for one to see his great-grandsons. In an Aramaic tomb inscription from Nerab dating to the seventh century b.c., Agbar observes that he was surrounded by “children of the fourth generation” as he lay on his death bed (see *ANET* 661). The language of the text differs from {{Exodus 34:7|Exod 34:7}}, the sons are the first generation, the grandsons (literally, “sons of the sons”) the second, great-grandsons the third, and great-great-grandsons the fourth. One could argue that formulation in {{Deuteronomy 5:9|Deut 5:9}} (see also {{Exodus 20:5|Exod 20:5}}) is elliptical/abbreviated or that the text suffers from an accidental scribal omission (the repetition of the words “sons” would invite accidental omission).

*Study note:* Verses {{Deuteronomy 6:4|4-5}} constitute the so-called *Shema* (after the first word שְׁמַע, shemaʿ, “hear”), widely regarded as the very heart of Jewish confession and faith. When Jesus was asked what was the greatest commandment of all, he quoted this text ({{Matthew 22:37|Matt 22:37-38}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the Lord, our God, the Lord, one.” (1) One option is to translate: “The Lord is our God, the Lord alone” (cf. NAB, NRSV, NLT). This would be an affirmation that the Lord was the sole object of their devotion. This interpretation finds support from the appeals to loyalty that follow (vv. {{Deuteronomy 6:5|5}}, {{Deuteronomy 6:14|14}}). (2) Another option is to translate: “The Lord is our God, the Lord is unique.” In this case the text would be affirming the people’s allegiance to the Lord, as well as the Lord’s superiority to all other gods. It would also imply that he is the only one worthy of their worship. Support for this view comes from parallel texts such as {{Deuteronomy 7:9|Deut 7:9}} and {{Deuteronomy 10:17|10:17}}, as well as the use of “one” in Song 6:8-9, where the starstruck lover declares that his beloved is unique (literally, “one,” that is, “one of a kind”) when compared to all other women.

*Translator's note:* The verb אָהֵב (ʾahev, “to love”) in this setting communicates not so much an emotional idea as one of covenant commitment. To love the Lord is to be absolutely loyal and obedient to him in every respect, a truth Jesus himself taught (cf. {{John 14:15|John 14:15}}). See also the note on the word “loved” in {{Deuteronomy 4:37|Deut 4:37}}.

It is therefore best in most cases to translate נֶפֶשׁ (nefesh) as “being” or the like. See H. W. Wolff, *Anthropology of the Old Testament*, 10-25; D. Fredericks, *NIDOTTE* 3:133-34.

It was the hypocritical practice of wearing these without heartfelt sincerity that caused Jesus to speak scathingly about them (cf. {{Matthew 23:5|Matt 23:5}}).

*Study note:* *Hittites*. The center of Hittite power was in Anatolia (central modern Turkey). In the Late Bronze Age (1550-1200 b.c.) they were at their zenith, establishing outposts and colonies near and far. Some elements were obviously in Canaan at the time of the Conquest (1400-1350 b.c.).

*Study note:* *Girgashites*. These cannot be ethnically identified and are unknown outside the OT. They usually appear in such lists only when the intention is to have seven groups in all (see also the note on the word “seven” later in this verse).

*Study note:* *Amorites*. Originally from the upper Euphrates region (*Amurru*), the Amorites appear to have migrated into Canaan beginning in 2200 b.c. or thereabouts.

*Study note:* *Canaanites*. These were the indigenous peoples of the land, going back to the beginning of recorded history (ca. 3000 b.c.). The OT identifies them as descendants of Ham ({{Genesis 10:6|Gen 10:6}}), the only Hamites to have settled north and east of Egypt.

*Study note:* *Perizzites*. This is probably a subgroup of Canaanites ({{Genesis 13:7|Gen 13:7}}; {{Genesis 34:30|34:30}}).

*Study note:* *Hivites*. These are usually thought to be the same as the Hurrians, a people well-known in ancient Near Eastern texts. They are likely identical to the Horites (see note on the term “Horites” in {{Deuteronomy 2:12|Deut 2:12}}).

*Study note:* *Jebusites*. These inhabited the hill country, particularly in and about Jerusalem (cf. {{Numbers 13:29|Num 13:29}}; {{Joshua 15:8|Josh 15:8}}; {{2 Samuel 5:6|2 Sam 5:6}}; {{2 Samuel 24:16|24:16}}).

*Study note:* *Seven*. This is an ideal number in the OT, one symbolizing fullness or completeness. Therefore, the intent of the text here is not to be precise and list all of Israel’s enemies but simply to state that Israel will have a full complement of foes to deal with. For other lists of Canaanites, some with fewer than seven peoples, see {{Exodus 3:8|Exod 3:8}}; {{Exodus 13:5|13:5}}; {{Exodus 23:23|23:23}}, {{Exodus 23:28|28}}; {{Exodus 33:2|33:2}}; {{Exodus 34:11|34:11}}; {{Deuteronomy 20:17|Deut 20:17}}; {{Joshua 3:10|Josh 3:10}}; {{Joshua 9:1|9:1}}; {{Joshua 24:11|24:11}}. Moreover, the “Table of Nations” ({{Genesis 10:15|Gen 10:15-19}}) suggests that all of these (possibly excepting the Perizzites) were offspring of Canaan and therefore Canaanites.

At this point, the Hebrew also switches from the plural (see previous clause) to the singular in reference to the Canaanite sons and daughters. While the principle applies to everyone in the nation, the rhetorical presentation is of an individual father making a decision about his specific child and a particular potential spouse.

*Study note:* *Sacred pillars*. The Hebrew word (מַצֵּבֹת, matsevot) denotes a standing pillar, usually made of stone. Its purpose was to mark the presence of a shrine or altar thought to have been visited by deity. Though sometimes associated with pure worship of the Lord ({{Genesis 28:18|Gen 28:18}}, {{Genesis 28:22|22}}; {{Genesis 31:13|31:13}}; {{Genesis 35:14|35:14}}; {{Exodus 24:4|Exod 24:4}}), these pillars were usually associated with pagan cults and rituals ({{Exodus 23:24|Exod 23:24}}; {{Exodus 34:13|34:13}}; {{Deuteronomy 12:3|Deut 12:3}}; {{1 Kings 14:23|1 Kgs 14:23}}; {{2 Kings 17:10|2 Kgs 17:10}}; Hos 3:4; 10:1; Jer 43:13).

*Study note:* *Sacred Asherah poles*. A leading deity of the Canaanite pantheon was Asherah, wife/sister of El and goddess of fertility. She was commonly worshiped at shrines in or near groves of evergreen trees, or, failing that, at places marked by wooden poles (Hebrew אֲשֵׁרִים [ʾasherim], as here). They were to be burned or cut down ({{Deuteronomy 12:3|Deut 12:3}}; {{Deuteronomy 16:21|16:21}}; {{Judges 6:25|Judg 6:25}}, {{Judges 6:28|28}}, {{Judges 6:30|30}}; {{2 Kings 18:4|2 Kgs 18:4}}).

*Study note:* *Redeeming you from the place of slavery*. The Hebrew verb translated “redeeming” (from the root פָּדָה, padah) has the idea of redemption by the payment of a ransom. The initial symbol of this was the Passover lamb, offered by Israel to the Lord as ransom in exchange for deliverance from bondage and death ({{Exodus 12:1|Exod 12:1-14}}). Later, the firstborn sons of Israel, represented by the Levites, became the ransom ({{Numbers 3:11|Num 3:11-13}}). These were all types of the redemption effected by the death of Christ who described his atoning work as “a ransom for many” ({{Matthew 20:28|Matt 20:28}}; cf. 1 Pet 1:18).

Rather, the sense is that God himself—not Moses in any way—was responsible for the composition of the Ten Commandments (cf. {{Exodus 31:18|Exod 31:18}}; {{Exodus 32:16|32:16}}; {{Exodus 34:1|34:1}}).

*Study note:* *The same words*. The care with which the replacement copy must be made underscores the importance of verbal precision in relaying the Lord’s commandments.

*Study note:* *Acacia wood* (*Heb* “shittim wood”). This is wood from the acacia, the most common timber tree of the Sinai region. Most likely it is the species *Acacia raddiana* because this has the largest trunk. See F. N. Hepper, *Illustrated Encyclopedia of Bible Plants*, 63.

*Study note:* *Beeroth Bene Jaakan*. This Hebrew name could be translated “the wells of Bene Jaakan” or “the wells of the sons of Jaakan,” a site whose location cannot be determined (cf. {{Numbers 33:31|Num 33:31-32}}; 1 Chr 1:42).

*Study note:* *Moserah*. Since Aaron in other texts ({{Numbers 20:28|Num 20:28}}; {{Numbers 33:38|33:38}}) is said to have died on Mount Hor, this must be the Arabah region in which Hor was located.

*Study note:* *Gudgodah*. This is probably the same as Haggidgad, which is also associated with Jotbathah ({{Numbers 33:33|Num 33:33}}).

*Study note:* *Jotbathah*. This place, whose Hebrew name can be translated “place of wadis,” is possibly modern Ain Tabah, just north of Eilat, or Tabah, 6.5 mi (11 km) south of Eilat on the west shore of the Gulf of Aqaba.

*Study note:* *The* Lord *set apart the tribe of Levi*. This was not the initial commissioning of the tribe of Levi to this ministry (cf. {{Numbers 3:11|Num 3:11-13}}; {{Numbers 8:12|8:12-26}}), but with Aaron’s death it seemed appropriate to Moses to reiterate Levi’s responsibilities. There is no reference in the Book of Numbers to this having been done, but the account of Eleazar’s succession to the priesthood there ({{Numbers 20:25|Num 20:25-28}}) would provide a setting for this to have occurred.

*Study note:* *To formulate blessings*. The most famous example of this is the priestly “blessing formula” of {{Numbers 6:24|Num 6:24-26}}.

*Study note:* *Levi has no allotment or inheritance*. As the priestly tribe, Levi would have no land allotment except for forty-eight towns set apart for their use ({{Numbers 35:1|Num 35:1-8}}; {{Joshua 21:1|Josh 21:1-42}}). But theirs was a far greater inheritance, for the Lord himself was their apportionment, that is, service to him would be their full-time and lifelong privilege ({{Numbers 18:20|Num 18:20-24}}; {{Deuteronomy 18:2|Deut 18:2}}; {{Joshua 13:33|Josh 13:33}}).

Just as that act signified total covenant obedience, so spiritual circumcision (cleansing of the heart) signifies more internally a commitment to be pliable and obedient to the will of God (cf. {{Deuteronomy 30:6|Deut 30:6}}; Jer 4:4; 9:26).
